Proof:
By the definition of multiindex notation for exponentiation, the expression $(x + y)^\alpha$ can be expanded as a product of scalar terms:
$$(x + y)^\alpha = \prod_{j=1}^n (x_j + y_j)^{\alpha_j}$$

Since each component $\alpha_j$ is a non-negative integer ($\alpha_j \ge 0$), we can apply the standard one-dimensional Binomial Theorem to each factor $(x_j + y_j)^{\alpha_j}$:
$$(x_j + y_j)^{\alpha_j} = \sum_{\beta_j = 0}^{\alpha_j} \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j}$$

Substituting this into the initial product gives:
$$(x + y)^\alpha = \prod_{j=1}^n \left( \sum_{\beta_j = 0}^{\alpha_j} \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right)$$

By the generalized distributive law (expanding the product of finite sums), we can interchange the product and the summations. The product of $n$ independent sums, each indexed by $\beta_j$ ranging from $0$ to $\alpha_j$, is equal to a multiple sum over all possible combinations of the indices $(\beta_1, \dots, \beta_n)$:
$$\prod_{j=1}^n \left( \sum_{\beta_j = 0}^{\alpha_j} \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right) = \sum_{\beta_1 = 0}^{\alpha_1} \sum_{\beta_2 = 0}^{\alpha_2} \cdots \sum_{\beta_n = 0}^{\alpha_n} \prod_{j=1}^n \left( \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right)$$

The condition that each index $\beta_j$ ranges from $0$ to $\alpha_j$ for all $j \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ is precisely the definition of the multiindex inequality $0 \le \beta \le \alpha$, where $\beta = (\beta_1, \dots, \beta_n)$. Thus, the $n$-fold multiple summation can be concisely written as a single sum over the multiindex $\beta$:
$$\sum_{0 \le \beta \le \alpha} \prod_{j=1}^n \left( \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right)$$

Because the scalar terms in the product commute, we can rearrange the factors inside the product:
$$\prod_{j=1}^n \left( \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right) = \left( \prod_{j=1}^n \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} \right) \left( \prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{\beta_j} \right) \left( \prod_{j=1}^n y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right)$$

Now, we apply the definitions of multiindex notation to each of these products:
1. The multiindex binomial coefficient is defined as $\binom{\alpha}{\beta} = \prod_{j=1}^n \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j}$.
2. Multiindex exponentiation on $x$ is defined as $x^\beta = \prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{\beta_j}$.
3. Similarly, multiindex exponentiation on $y$ is $y^{\alpha - \beta} = \prod_{j=1}^n y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j}$.

Substituting these definitions back into the general term of the sum yields:
$$\left( \prod_{j=1}^n \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} \right) \left( \prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{\beta_j} \right) \left( \prod_{j=1}^n y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right) = \binom{\alpha}{\beta} x^\beta y^{\alpha - \beta}$$

Therefore, the entire expansion simplifies exactly to the desired expression:
$$(x + y)^\alpha = \sum_{0 \le \beta \le \alpha} \binom{\alpha}{\beta} x^\beta y^{\alpha - \beta}$$
This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$
